r_toxic: Win. At PFA 0.05 DeepQCD catches 46% of runs (seeds 0.44–0.48). The best rule (price move over 5 seconds) catches 21%, the CUSUM 16%, and the logistic model with the same features but no memory 14%. At PFA 0.01 it is 0.34 against 0.12. Most of the gain is on the smaller runs (15–20 bps: 0.43 against at most 0.13), which are the ones simple alarms miss; on runs of 30 bps or more everyone catches about 0.7. DeepQCD rings a little later (median 22 seconds into a run that lasts about 35), but it catches so many more that it avoids 2.6–2.7 bps of adverse move per run on average, against 1.6 for the best rule and 1.5 for the CUSUM: about 60% more. With 40 days of data it caught 0.35, so more history helped.
r_amlworld: Win at the strict level, tie at the loose one. AMLworld launders mostly through ACH (87% of laundering transfers, 12% of all). A single rule, ACH to or from a new counterparty, catches 64% at PFA 0.05, level with DeepQCD (0.62; seeds 0.60–0.64) and the logistic model (0.60). But that rule is yes-or-no, so it cannot work below its own false-alarm rate: at PFA 0.01 it catches nothing, while DeepQCD catches 41% (seeds 0.36–0.44), the logistic model 27% and the CUSUM 2%. A bank that has to keep alerts down gets most from the sequence model. Laundering that does not start with ACH (15% of accounts) is missed by everything (at most 0.05).
r_mm: Alarms help; DeepQCD adds little here. Quoting against every trade loses 12.7 cents per $100 of volume: over 5 minutes, Polymarket's takers are on average better informed than a passive market maker. The surprise is churn. Minutes with a churning wallet are the most toxic (−0.37 cents per share on our fills, against −0.23 during metaorders and −0.06 otherwise), so the churners here are mostly skilled scalpers, not harmless wash traders. Stepping back on the metaorder alarm (only on the side being hit) cuts the loss to 3.8 cents with 59% of the volume. Stepping back on the churn alarm or on either alarm reaches break-even (−0.07 and +0.04 cents) with about a third of the volume. But a plain "busy" rule gets almost the same (−0.16), because most of the volume trades in busy minutes. Only perfect knowledge of metaorders makes money (+1.9 cents with 71% of the volume), and the gap to it is what a better metaorder detector is worth. The replay ignores queue position and Polymarket's liquidity rewards, which pay real makers for quoting.
r_squeeze: Tie. DeepQCD catches 76% of rallies at PFA 0.05 (seeds 0.75–0.77), the CUSUM 75%, and a 2-day-return rule and the logistic model 69%. At PFA 0.01 it is 0.70 against 0.67. A squeeze is mostly one thing, the price going up, which a short window over returns already sees. The value is the same story: alarms come about 5 days in, with about 17% of a 93% rally left, saving about 13% per rally for DeepQCD, the CUSUM and the return rule alike. The volume-spike rule catches only 41% but much earlier (43% of the rally still ahead) and saves the most, 17.6% per rally. For short sellers, speed beats coverage, and volume comes before price.
r_credit: Tie. At PFA 0.05 DeepQCD flags 31% of defaulters, the CUSUM 30%, the logistic model 25% and "months late now" 10%. At PFA 0.2, the level credit teams work at, everyone is at 0.62–0.64 and the one-line "months late now" rule is as good as any. Six monthly steps are too short a history for memory to matter, and the strongest signal, being late already, is in the current month.
r_fraud: Win, most at strict false-alarm levels. At PFA 0.01 DeepQCD catches 54% of fraud bursts (seeds 0.50–0.61), against 33% for the logistic model, 28% for the CUSUM and at most 9% for any rule. At PFA 0.05 it is 0.69 against 0.66 and 0.64. Card issuers operate at very low false-positive rates, so the 0.01 column is the one that matters to them. The gain is largest when the fraud starts online (0.76 against 0.60 for the logistic model): an online purchase is normal for some cards and alarming for others, and only the card's history tells which. When the fraud starts in person, the CUSUM (0.77) and the logistic model (0.73) do better than DeepQCD (0.61). Every detector, when it catches a burst, lets one fraudulent transaction through before the alarm (median).
